mainTopic: Cancelling forbidden food in sixty: tasting, salted meat with the גיד הנשה, how to measure, and the cases of the גיד, כחל and egg
overview: This amud finishes the rules for forbidden food that gets mixed into permitted food. When the two foods taste different, we rely on tasting: a Jew tastes if the mixture is permitted to him, and a קפילא (non-Jewish cook) tastes if it might be forbidden. When tasting is impossible, we need sixty times as much permitted food. Next comes a real case: thighs were salted with the גיד הנשה still inside. רבינא forbade them, while רב אחא בר רב אשי and רב אשי permitted them. רבינא's view is left with a קשיא, because שמואל's rule מליח כרותח means salted food is like roasted food, and roasted meat only needs peeling. The גמרא then teaches what counts toward the sixty (רבי חנינא) and that every forbidden food is measured as if it were as strong as onion or leek (רבי יוחנן). רב נחמן rules on the גיד, the כחל and a non-kosher egg, and the גמרא explains that the כחל itself stays forbidden like a piece of נבלה. Finally, רב אידי בר אבין asks whether an egg gives off taste at all, and אביי's answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The Sages' measure of sixty and when we rely on tasting
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן set sixty as the measure for cancelling forbidden food. When the two foods taste different, we decide by tasting: a Jew tastes if the mixture is permitted to him, and a non-Jewish cook (קפילא) tastes if it might be forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the רבנן said: sixty. Therefore, when one kind of food is mixed with a different kind: if the mixture is permitted, we go by taste; if it is forbidden, we go by a non-Jewish cook (קפילא).
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא states the רבנן's measure of sixty and then explains how tasting works in practice when the two foods have different flavors.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the forbidden food has a different flavor from the permitted food, we can simply check whether its taste comes through. A Jew may only taste the mixture if he is allowed to eat it. If it might really be forbidden, a non-Jewish cook (קפילא) tastes it for us.

keyTerms.meaning: Sixty: the forbidden food is cancelled if there is sixty times as much permitted food
One kind of food mixed with a different kind, so the flavors are different
Taste: checking whether the forbidden flavor can be detected
A non-Jewish cook who tastes the mixture
A permitted case / a forbidden case

phrases.english: And the Sages said: in sixty.
phrases.notes: This means sixty times as much permitted food as forbidden food.

phrases.english: Therefore, a type mixed with what is not its type:
where it is permitted, we go by tasting,
where it is forbidden, we go by a non-Jewish cook.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַאֲמוּר רַבָּנַן בְּשִׁשִּׁים. הִלְכָּךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier discussion, from before this section, about how forbidden food gets cancelled in a mixture.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The rabbinic measure is sixty. When the flavors differ, tasting decides: a Jew tastes a permitted mixture, and a קפילא tastes a possibly forbidden one.

steps.title: When tasting is impossible, we use sixty
steps.stepSummary: When the two foods are the same kind, the forbidden taste cannot be detected. When the mixture might be forbidden and no non-Jewish cook is available, tasting is also impossible. In both cases we use the measure of sixty.
steps.simpleTranslation: And when a type is mixed with its own type, where taste cannot be checked, or when a type is mixed with a different type in a forbidden case and there is no non-Jewish cook, we use sixty.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the practical rule. Whenever tasting cannot work, we go by sixty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two situations make tasting useless. In מין במינו, both foods taste the same, so nobody can tell whether the forbidden part comes through. In the other case, nobody suitable is available to taste. The fallback in both cases is the fixed measure of sixty.

keyTerms.meaning: A food mixed with the same kind of food
To determine the taste, to figure out whether the forbidden flavor is there
There is not / it is not possible

steps.whatToRemember: In practice: when the flavors differ, tasting decides (a Jew if the mixture is permitted to him, a קפילא if it might be forbidden). When tasting is impossible (מין במינו, or no קפילא available), we need sixty times as much permitted food.

phrases.english: And a type mixed with its own type,
where it is not possible to determine the taste,

phrases.aramaic: אִי נָמֵי מִין בְּשֶׁאֵינוֹ מִינוֹ דְּאִיסּוּרָא,
phrases.english: or a type with what is not its type, in a forbidden case,
where there is no non-Jewish cook: in sixty.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִין בְּמִינוֹ, דְּלֵיכָּא לְמֵיקַם אַטַּעְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the practical rule from step 1 by covering the cases where tasting cannot work.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Whenever tasting is impossible, the mixture is permitted only if there is sixty times as much permitted food.

steps.title: Thighs salted with the sciatic nerve inside: a dispute
steps.stepSummary: Animal thighs were salted in the house of the ריש גלותא with the גיד הנשה still inside. רבינא forbade the meat, and רב אחא בר רב אשי permitted it.
steps.simpleTranslation: There were thighs that were salted in the house of the ריש גלותא with the גיד הנשה inside. רבינא forbade them; רב אחא בר רב אשי permitted them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new topic with a real-life case. Two אמוראים disagree about whether salting the meat with the גיד הנשה inside makes it forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whether salting has the same effect as cooking, which would let the taste of the גיד spread into the meat. רבינא treats it as forbidden. רב אחא בר רב אשי says it stays permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: The גיד הנשה, the sciatic nerve that may not be eaten
The Exilarch, the leader of the Jews in Babylonia

phrases.english: There were those thighs
that were salted in the house of the Exilarch
with the sciatic nerve,
Ravina forbade them,

phrases.aramaic: רַב אַחָא בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי שָׁרֵי.
phrases.english: Rav Acha bar Rav Ashi permitted them.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנְהוּ אַטְמָהָתָא דְּאִימְּלִיחוּ בֵּי רֵישׁ גָּלוּתָא בְּגִידָא נַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: the halacha of meat salted together with the גיד הנשה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is a dispute: רבינא forbids thighs salted with the גיד הנשה, and רב אחא בר רב אשי permits them.

steps.title: מר בר רב אשי reports that his father permitted it
steps.stepSummary: The people asked מר בר רב אשי. He told them that his father, רב אשי, permitted meat in this situation.
steps.simpleTranslation: They came and asked מר בר רב אשי. He said to them: My father permitted it.
steps.whatsHappening: To settle the dispute, they ask מר בר רב אשי, and he quotes his father's ruling that the meat is permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This adds the authority of רב אשי on the side of permitting. It supports רב אחא בר רב אשי against רבינא.

phrases.aramaic: אֲתוֹ שַׁיְילוּהּ לְמָר בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי,
phrases.english: They came and asked Mar bar Rav Ashi,
He said to them: My father permitted it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲתוֹ שַׁיְילוּהּ לְמָר בַּר רַב אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the dispute from step 3 by quoting רב אשי's ruling.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב אשי permitted thighs salted with the גיד הנשה inside.

steps.title: Asking רבינא for his reason: is salted like boiling hot?
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בר רב asks רבינא why he forbids the meat. He suggests the reason might be שמואל's rule that salted food counts as boiling hot and pickled food counts as cooked.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא בר רב said to רבינא: What is your reasoning? Is it because שמואל said: salted food is like boiling hot food, and pickled food is like cooked food?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא בר רב asks רבינא to explain his ruling and offers a possible source, שמואל's rule about salting. This sets up the next move, where that reasoning will be examined.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If salting counts like boiling heat, then the גיד's taste would spread into the meat as if they were cooked together, and the meat would be forbidden. The question puts רבינא's reasoning on the table so the גמרא can test whether שמואל's rule really applies here.

keyTerms.meaning: Salted food counts like boiling hot food
Food soaked (pickled) in liquid counts like cooked food

steps.whyThisMatters: The rule מליח כרותח is a basic idea in the halachos of salting meat and mixtures. It is the reason salting can make forbidden flavor spread just as cooking does.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בַּר רַב לְרָבִינָא:
phrases.english: Rav Acha bar Rav said to Ravina:
What is your reasoning?
Is it because Shmuel said:
Salted food is like boiling hot food,
pickled food is like cooked food?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בַּר רַב לְרָבִינָא: מַאי דַּעְתָּיךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns back to רבינא's side of the dispute and asks for the source of his ruling.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason רבינא forbids the salted thighs, and whether it comes from שמואל's rule that salted food is like boiling hot food.

steps.title: Roasted thigh with the nerve only needs peeling
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בר רב continues his challenge. שמואל also said a thigh roasted with the גיד הנשה only needs to be peeled. If salted food is like roasted-hot food, salted meat should also only need peeling, not be fully forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't שמואל say: they only taught that the whole thigh is forbidden when it was cooked with the nerve inside. If it was roasted with the nerve inside, you peel away the meat and eat it until you reach the nerve.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second statement of שמואל to finish the challenge against רבינא. Roasting with the nerve does not forbid the whole thigh.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 5 we heard שמואל's rule that salted food counts as boiling hot. Here we learn that roasting, a kind of 'hot,' only affects the meat near the nerve, so you peel and eat. Put together, salted meat should be like roasted meat, so it should be permitted after peeling, against רבינא.

keyTerms.meaning: They only taught [this rule] in the case of…

phrases.english: But didn't Shmuel say:
They only taught this when it was cooked inside it,
but if it was roasted inside it,
he peels and eats until he reaches the nerve.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָאָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב אחא בר רב's challenge begun in step 5 by adding a second rule of שמואל.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבינא's ruling forbidding the salted thighs
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Salted is like hot-roasted, and roasted with the nerve only needs peeling, so salted should only need peeling.

steps.title: Maybe 'hot' means hot like cooked food
steps.stepSummary: A possible defense of רבינא: when שמואל said salted is 'like boiling hot,' perhaps he meant hot like cooked food, which forbids the whole thigh.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you would say: what did שמואל mean by 'like boiling hot'? He meant like boiling hot food that is cooked.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests a way to save רבינא. Maybe 'hot' means cooked-hot, not roasted-hot.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If salting is like cooking, the taste of the nerve spreads through the whole thigh, just as it does in cooking. Then רבינא would be right to forbid all the meat. The גמרא raises this only to reject it in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you would say (introduces a suggested answer)

phrases.english: And if you would say,
what is the 'like boiling hot' that he said?
phrases.notes: This points back to שמואל's rule from step 5, that salted food counts as boiling hot.

phrases.english: Like boiling hot of cooked food!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attempts to defend רבינא against the challenge of steps 5-6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting a word ('hot') in שמואל's rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Salted is like roasted-hot, so peeling is enough.
steps.terutzMaskana: Salted is like cooked-hot, so the whole thigh is forbidden.

steps.title: The defense fails, and the question stands
steps.stepSummary: The defense is rejected. שמואל separately said 'pickled is like cooked.' So when he said 'salted is like hot,' he must have meant roasted-hot. רבינא is left with an unanswered difficulty.
steps.simpleTranslation: But since שמואל said that pickled food is like cooked food, we can infer that by 'boiling hot' he meant hot like roasted food. This is a difficulty.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the defense from step 7 and ends the discussion with 'קשיא': רבינא's ruling remains challenged.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל used two different comparisons: pickled is 'like cooked' and salted is 'like hot.' If both meant cooking, he would have used the same word. So 'hot' must mean roasting. That brings back the peeling rule and leaves רבינא's ruling with no answer.

keyTerms.meaning: It is a difficulty (unresolved, but not a full refutation)

steps.whatToRemember: רבינא's ruling forbidding the salted thighs ends with 'קשיא.' Salted food is like roasted-hot food, and a roasted thigh only needs peeling.
steps.confusionAlert: 'קשיא' at the end is not the same as 'תיובתא.' It means the question is strong and unanswered, but the opinion is not formally knocked out.

phrases.english: But from the fact that he said
pickled is like cooked,
it follows that he meant boiling hot of roasted food.
It is a difficulty.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא מִדְּקָאָמַר כָּבוּשׁ הֲרֵי הוּא כִּמְבוּשָּׁל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the defense of step 7 and closes the branch with an unanswered difficulty.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The reading of 'hot' as 'hot like cooked'
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: שמואל already said pickled is like cooked, so 'hot' must refer to something different: roasting.

steps.title: What we count when measuring sixty
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא teaches that when measuring sixty against forbidden food, we count the broth, the residue, the pieces, and the pot.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא said: when they measure sixty, they count the broth, the residue at the bottom, the pieces of meat, and the pot.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the rule of sixty from steps 1-2. Now it explains what goes into the permitted side of the count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everything in the pot that could take on the forbidden taste counts toward the sixty, not just the solid meat. That makes it easier to reach sixty. Exactly what 'the pot' means is explained in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: They measure / assess (the ratio of sixty)
Residue / thick deposits at the bottom of the pot

phrases.english: Rabbi Chanina said:
When they measure, they measure
phrases.notes: He means measuring whether the permitted food is sixty times the forbidden food.

phrases.english: with the broth and the residue
and the pieces and the pot.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא כְּשֶׁהֵן מְשַׁעֲרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the גיד הנשה discussion and returns to the measure of sixty from steps 1-2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Broth, residue, pieces, and the pot all count toward the sixty.

steps.title: Two views on what 'the pot' means
steps.stepSummary: There are two opinions on 'the pot' in רבי חנינא's list. Some say it means the pot's own material. Others say it means the food the pot's walls have absorbed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: the pot itself. Others say: what the pot has absorbed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא clarifies one word in רבי חנינא's list, 'the pot,' and gives two opinions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By the first view, the actual size of the pot counts toward the sixty. By the second view, only the permitted food soaked into the pot's walls counts. The second view is stricter, since it adds less to the permitted side.

phrases.english: There are those who say: the pot itself,
and there are those who say: what the pot absorbed.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי בִּקְדֵרָה עַצְמָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the last item ('the pot') in רבי חנינא's list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'The pot' means either the pot's own material or the food absorbed in it (two views).

steps.title: Measure every forbidden food as if it were onion or leek
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן rules that every forbidden food in the תורה is measured as if it had the strong taste of onion or leek.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבהו said in the name of רבי יוחנן: all the prohibitions of the תורה are measured as if they were onion and leek.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds another rule about measuring בטול: how strong to assume the forbidden taste is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Onion and leek have a sharp taste that spreads easily. Imagining the forbidden food as that strong means we are strict. If that much onion or leek would give the dish taste, the mixture is forbidden.
steps.whatToRemember: When measuring whether forbidden food gives taste, we picture it as strong as onion or leek, which is a strict approach.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Abbahu said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
All prohibitions that are in the Torah
we measure them
phrases.notes: Some versions say 'מְשַׁעֲרִינַן' in round brackets; the words in square brackets are the corrected wording. Both mean 'we measure.'

phrases.english: as if they were onion and leek.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן כׇּל אִיסּוּרִין שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another measuring rule alongside רבי חנינא's.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: All תורה prohibitions are measured as if they had the strong taste of onion or leek.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a strict standard for judging whether forbidden food has given taste to a mixture.

steps.title: Why not measure as if it were pepper?
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא challenges אביי: if we treat forbidden food as having a strong taste, why not treat it like pepper and spices, which are never cancelled out?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא said to אביי: Then let us measure forbidden foods as if they were pepper and spices, which are not cancelled out even in a thousand times their amount!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא pushes back on רבי יוחנן's rule from the previous step. If we are being strict and treating forbidden food as very strong, why stop at onion and leek?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן said every forbidden food is measured as if it had the strong taste of onion or leek. רבי אבא points out that pepper and spices are even stronger, so strong that even a thousand times as much food won't cancel them. If we want to be safe, why not use the strongest standard?

phrases.english: Rabbi Abba said to Abaye:
But let us measure them as if they were pepper and spices,
phrases.notes: "Them" means all the forbidden foods from רבי יוחנן's rule in the last step.

phrases.english: which are not cancelled out even in a thousand!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְשַׁעֲרִינְהוּ בְּפִלְפְּלִין וְתַבְלִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the onion-and-leek standard set by רבי יוחנן in step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's rule that forbidden foods are measured like onion and leek.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If we assume a strong taste to be strict, the strongest known tastes (pepper and spices) should be the standard, and those are never cancelled.

steps.title: Nothing forbidden is stronger than onion and leek
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that the חכמים found that no forbidden food gives off more taste than onion and leek.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: The חכמים determined that among forbidden foods, nothing gives off more taste than onion and leek.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי defends רבי יוחנן's rule. The onion-and-leek standard is not a guess; it is the strongest taste the חכמים found among forbidden foods.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question was why we don't use pepper as the measure. אביי answers that the measure only needs to cover the strongest forbidden food, and among forbidden foods none is stronger than onion and leek. So that is the right level of strictness, and the challenge is answered.

keyTerms.meaning: Gives off taste into the mixture

steps.whatToRemember: Forbidden food is measured as if it had the taste of onion or leek, because the חכמים found no forbidden food with a stronger taste.

phrases.english: He said to him: The Sages determined
that among forbidden foods, nothing gives off taste
more than onion and leek.

steps.triggerLanguage: שִׁיעֲרוּ חֲכָמִים דְּאֵין נוֹתֵן טַעַם בְּאִיסּוּרִין יוֹתֵר מִבָּצָל וְקַפְלוֹט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי אבא's challenge from step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual limit: the standard matches the strongest taste actually found among forbidden foods.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Maybe we should use the strongest taste of all, like pepper, which is never cancelled.
steps.terutzMaskana: The standard only has to match forbidden foods, and none of them is stronger than onion and leek.

steps.title: Three cases: what counts toward the sixty
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן rules that a גיד הנשה, a כחל, and a non-kosher egg each need ששים, but only the כחל is counted as part of the ששים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: A גיד needs ששים, and the גיד itself is not counted. A כחל needs ששים, and the כחל is counted. An egg needs ששים, and the egg is not counted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching about cancelling forbidden food in ששים. רב נחמן lists three cases and tells us whether the forbidden item itself helps make up the ששים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For the גיד and the egg, the item itself is the forbidden thing, so it cannot help cancel itself and is not counted. The כחל is different: the udder itself is meat, and only the milk inside it is the problem. So the udder's meat joins the rest of the meat in cancelling that milk.

keyTerms.meaning: The גיד הנשה, the forbidden sciatic nerve
An udder, meat that has milk inside it
Part of the count (counted toward the ששים)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the כחל is counted because it is less forbidden. It is counted because the udder is meat, and the only forbidden part is the milk inside it.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said: A sciatic nerve is cancelled in sixty,
and the nerve is not part of the count;
an udder is cancelled in sixty, and the udder is part of the count;
phrases.notes: The udder's meat is fine; only the milk inside it is the problem, so the meat helps cancel that milk.

phrases.aramaic: בֵּיצָה בְּשִׁשִּׁים, וְאֵין בֵּיצָה מִן הַמִּנְיָן.
phrases.english: an egg is cancelled in sixty, and the egg is not part of the count.
phrases.notes: This means the egg of a non-kosher bird.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from how strong a forbidden taste is to what is counted toward the ששים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: גיד and a non-kosher egg need ששים not counting themselves; a כחל needs ששים and is counted itself.
steps.whyThisMatters: These three cases show the key idea: whatever is itself forbidden can't help cancel itself, but permitted parts of the same item can.

steps.title: The udder itself stays forbidden
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק בריה דרב משרשיא adds that even when the meat around it is permitted, the כחל itself is forbidden, and if it falls into another pot it forbids that pot too.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק בריה דרב משרשיא said: The כחל itself is forbidden, and if it falls into another pot, it makes that pot forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: This adds a limit to רב נחמן's כחל rule. The meat in the pot may be permitted, but the udder itself does not become permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן said the milk of the כחל can be cancelled in ששים of meat. רבי יצחק says that only saves the other meat, not the udder. The udder stays forbidden, and it is strong enough to forbid a second pot it falls into.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב מְשַׁרְשְׁיָא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzchak, son of Rav Mesharshiya, said:
And the udder itself is forbidden,
and if it fell into another pot, it makes it forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a limit to רב נחמן's כחל rule in step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The כחל itself stays forbidden even when the surrounding meat is permitted, and it forbids another pot it falls into.

steps.title: Measure against the whole udder or just its milk?
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי reports a question raised in רב כהנא's study hall about רב נחמן's כחל rule: when the udder is cooked with meat, do we need ששים against the whole udder, or only against the milk that came out of it?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: When we were in רב כהנא's study hall, we had a question: When we measure, do we measure against the udder itself, or against what came out of it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a question about how to measure the ששים for a כחל cooked with meat (רב נחמן's rule in step 14). The next step answers it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן said the כחל's milk is cancelled in ששים. The question is what the ששים is measured against. One option is the whole udder. The other is only the milk that actually came out of it into the pot, which is a much smaller amount.

keyTerms.meaning: We had a question (an open question)
What came out of it (the milk)

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הֲוֵינַן בֵּי רַב כָּהֲנָא, אִיבַּעְיָא לַן:
phrases.english: When we were in the study hall of Rav Kahana, we had a question:
When we measure, do we measure against it itself,
or do we measure against what came out of it?
phrases.notes: "What came out of it" means the milk that leaked out of the udder.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הֲוֵינַן בֵּי רַב כָּהֲנָא, אִיבַּעְיָא לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how the ששים for a כחל (רב נחמן's rule in step 14) is measured in the pot where it was cooked.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the ששים for a כחל cooked with meat is measured against the whole udder or only against the milk that came out of it.

steps.title: We measure against the whole udder
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that we obviously need ששים against the whole udder, because there is no way to know how much milk actually leaked out.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is obvious that we measure against the udder itself. If we tried to measure only by what came out of it, how would we know how much that was?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 16: the ששים is measured against the entire udder.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Measuring only against the milk that came out sounds more exact, but nobody can see or measure how much milk leaked into the food. Since that amount is unknown, the only workable measure is the whole udder.

keyTerms.meaning: We measure, we calculate the ratio
Against it itself, meaning the whole udder

phrases.english: It is obvious that we measure against it itself,
for if we measured by what came out of it –
how would we know?

steps.triggerLanguage: פְּשִׁיטָא דִּבְדִידֵיהּ מְשַׁעֲרִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question raised in Step 16.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether ששים is measured against the whole udder or only against the milk that came out.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Against the whole udder, because the amount of milk that came out cannot be known.

steps.title: Then why does the udder forbid a second pot?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: if we measure as though all the milk came out into the first pot, the udder should no longer forbid a second pot.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if so, when the udder falls into another pot, it should not make that pot forbidden!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from Step 17 by pointing to רבי יצחק's rule from Step 15.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Measuring against the whole udder treats it as if all of its milk was released into the first pot. If the milk is all gone, the udder should be harmless in a second pot. Yet Step 15 said it does forbid a second pot.

keyTerms.meaning: But if so (introduces a problem that follows from what was just said)

phrases.english: But if that is so,
if it fell into another pot – should it not forbid it?
phrases.notes: Since we treated all the milk as having come out in the first pot, nothing should be left to forbid the second pot.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the measuring method of Step 17 using the ruling in Step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that ששים is measured against the whole udder (Step 17).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Measuring against the whole udder assumes all its milk left in the first pot, so the udder should not forbid a second pot. That contradicts Step 15.

steps.title: The udder is treated like a piece of נבלה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that because the udder itself stays forbidden, the רבנן gave it the status of a piece of forbidden meat. It forbids the second pot on its own, not because of leftover milk.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since רב יצחק בריה דרב משרשיא said the udder itself is forbidden, the רבנן made it like a piece of נבלה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the challenge by explaining why the udder forbids a second pot even with no milk left.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second pot does not become forbidden because of milk. The udder itself became a forbidden item, like a piece of נבלה, and a forbidden piece forbids whatever it falls into.

keyTerms.meaning: The רבנן made it, gave it the status of

steps.whatToRemember: The ששים for a כחל is measured against the whole udder. The udder itself stays forbidden like a piece of נבלה, so it forbids any other pot it falls into.

phrases.aramaic: כֵּיוָן דְּאָמַר רַב יִצְחָק בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב מְשַׁרְשְׁיָא:
phrases.english: Since Rav Yitzchak son of Rav Mesharshiya said:
'And the udder itself is forbidden,'
the Rabbis made it like a piece of non-kosher meat.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֵּיוָן דְּאָמַר רַב יִצְחָק בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב מְשַׁרְשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the reason the udder forbids: it has its own forbidden status, not leftover milk.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The udder forbids a second pot only because milk is still inside it.
steps.terutzMaskana: The udder has the status of a piece of נבלה and forbids a second pot on its own.

steps.title: Quoting רב נחמן's rule about the egg
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes again the part of רב נחמן's ruling about a non-kosher egg: it needs ששים, and the egg is not counted in the ששים.
steps.simpleTranslation: An egg needs sixty, and the egg is not counted in the number.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the next move. It repeats the egg part of רב נחמן's ruling from Step 14 so it can question it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now the discussion was about the כחל. The גמרא now returns to the egg, whose rule is that the permitted food must be sixty times the egg without counting the egg itself.

keyTerms.meaning: An egg (here, of a non-kosher bird)
Cancelled out in sixty times its size

phrases.english: An egg is cancelled in sixty,
phrases.notes: This is the non-kosher egg from רב נחמן's ruling in Step 14.

phrases.english: and the egg is not counted in the number.

steps.triggerLanguage: בֵּיצָה בְּשִׁשִּׁים, וְאֵין בֵּיצָה מִן הַמִּנְיָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the כחל discussion and reopens the egg part of Step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A non-kosher egg needs ששים of permitted food, and the egg is not counted in that ששים.

steps.title: Does an egg even give off taste?
steps.stepSummary: רב אידי בר אבין challenges אביי: needing ששים implies the egg gives off taste, but people describe something tasteless as 'like egg-water.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אידי בר אבין said to אביי: Does this mean that an egg gives off taste? But people say, 'It's just like egg-water!'
steps.whatsHappening: רב אידי בר אבין attacks the egg ruling by pointing to the common saying that eggs are tasteless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ששים is only needed when something can give off taste. The everyday saying 'like egg-water' shows that people think of egg as having no taste, so why should it need ששים at all?

keyTerms.meaning: Egg-water, the water eggs were cooked in (a saying for something tasteless)

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אִידִי בַּר אָבִין לְאַבָּיֵי:
phrases.english: Rav Idi bar Avin said to Abaye:
Is this to say that it gives off taste?
But don't people say:
'It's just like egg-water!'
phrases.notes: People say this about food with no flavor, so it suggests eggs give off no taste.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְמֵימְרָא דְּיָהֲבָה טַעְמָא? וְהָא אָמְרִי אִינָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the egg rule quoted in Step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that a non-kosher egg needs ששים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: ששים is only needed for something that gives off taste, and the common saying shows egg is tasteless.

steps.title: אביי begins to explain the case
steps.stepSummary: אביי starts his answer by saying he will explain which specific case the egg ruling is about. The answer itself continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: Here, what are we dealing with?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי opens his answer by narrowing the case. The גמרא is setting up the next move, and the actual explanation comes right after this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'הכא במאי עסקינן' signals that the ruling does not cover every egg. It applies to a specific situation where the egg does give off taste, and that situation is spelled out next.

keyTerms.meaning: Here, what case are we dealing with? (introduces a narrower case to answer a challenge)

phrases.english: He said to him: Here, what are we dealing with?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the challenge of Step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (the answer is completed on the next amud).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ruling applies to any egg, even though eggs are generally tasteless.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ruling refers to a specific case, which is spelled out on the next amud.
